Muhammad Iqbal was a poet and philosopher, born in Sialkot in the Punjab in 1877, who wrote in Urdu and Persian and is seen as the spiritual father of Pakistan.

He studied in Lahore, then at Cambridge and in Germany, where he earned a doctorate. Early on he wrote Saare Jahan Se Achha, a patriotic song for all of India that is still sung there. Later his thinking turned toward the worldwide community of Muslims.

His great theme was khudi, the self: he urged Muslims to awaken their will and creative power rather than accept decline. His long Persian poem Asrar-i-Khudi of 1915 set this out. He took Rumi as his guide and wrote in Persian partly to reach readers across the Islamic world.

In 1930, as president of the Muslim League, he gave an address at Allahabad proposing a Muslim state in northwest India. He urged Jinnah to lead the cause. He died in Lahore in 1938, nine years before Pakistan was created. Pakistan counts him its national poet.
